title: Janapada of Kosala
capsule: Kosala was one of the sixteen mahājanapadas of ancient northern India, occupying the fertile Gangetic plain corresponding to modern Uttar Pradesh, with principal capitals at Śrāvastī and Ayodhyā. At its height in the sixth century BCE it was ruled by King Prasenajit (Pali: Pasenadi), a contemporary and patron of the Buddha who also oversaw the absorption of the Śākya republic—hometown of Siddhārtha Gautama—around 500 BCE. Kosala's significance lay as much in its patronage of early Buddhism and Jainism as in its military power, and it was the dominant state of the upper Ganges basin before Magadha's rise. By around 450 BCE Magadha under the Nanda predecessors had absorbed Kosala, ending the kingdom's independent existence.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Kosala's general extent in the middle Gangetic plain is attested in the Pali canon, the Mahābhārata, and Brahmanical texts, but precise territorial boundaries are reconstructed from literary geography rather than contemporaneous cartographic or epigraphic evidence.
